value.overview: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron is a secretive, medium-sized heron associated with clear, rocky streams in forested foothills and mountains. It usually hunts alone from the water’s edge or from rocks in fast-flowing channels. Adults have dark, finely pale-striped heads, necks, and upperparts, with a subdued reddish-brown belly and yellow eyes. Its compact shape and preference for rushing streams help distinguish it from other tiger-herons. The species is represented in Costa Rica by the salmoni form.
value.classification: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Tigrisoma. It is closely related to the Rufescent and Bare-throated Tiger-Herons.
value.identification: Adults are dark grayish to blackish overall, marked with narrow pale buff or whitish barring and streaking on the head, neck, back, and wings. The underparts are generally gray to dull cinnamon or reddish brown, while the flanks are gray. The iris is yellow, and the bill is short and stout, with a dark upper mandible and a yellowish-green lower base. Immatures are more heavily and evenly barred and can be difficult to separate from young tiger-herons without habitat clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica south through Panama and the Andes to Bolivia and northern Argentina, with a separate population in southeastern Brazil and northeastern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident, especially along the Caribbean-slope foothills from the Guanacaste Cordillera near Bijagua south toward Panama. It favors forested, hilly terrain with rocky, swift rivers and streams, commonly around 250–800 meters, although local records may reach about 2,400 meters. It may also use streams near artificial fishponds.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered resident in Costa Rica, with no well-established regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur along streams or with changes in water conditions and food availability.
value.breeding: Breeding information is poorly documented. The Fasciated Tiger-Heron builds a platform nest from sticks and woody vines, placed in vegetation near its forested river habitat. Reliable details about the Costa Rican breeding season, clutch size, incubation, and division of parental care remain limited. Because the species is local, secretive, and associated with difficult-to-access rushing streams, nesting behavior is observed much less often than its feeding behavior.
value.dietFeeding: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron feeds mainly in and beside fast-flowing streams. It stands motionless on rocks or banks, often with the neck partly extended, and seizes aquatic prey with a quick thrust of the bill. Its diet is believed to include small fish, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other stream-dwelling animals. Feeding is usually solitary, and birds may space themselves along productive stretches of river.
value.behavior: This heron is generally solitary or occurs in pairs and is often difficult to detect because it remains still among rocks, shadow, and streamside vegetation. It favors secluded sections of clear, rushing water and may perch or stand close to the channel while hunting. Individuals can occupy separate fishing sites along the same stream. When disturbed, it may retreat into dense vegetation or fly a short distance along the watercourse.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. Available assessments do not identify the species as globally threatened, but it is local and uncommon in parts of its range.
